content: Astigmatism, derived from the Greek words ameaning without and stigma meaning mark or spot, refers to a condition in optical systems where light rays propagating in two perpendicular planes come to focus at different points. This results in an inability to form a sharp image of a cross, as the vertical and horizontal lines will be in focus at two distinct distances. Forms of Astigmatism There are two primary forms of astigmatism: 1. Third-Order Aberration: This type of astigmatism occurs for objects or parts of objects that are off the optical axis, even in perfectly symmetrical optical systems. It is often referred to as monochromatic aberration because it can occur even with light of a single wavelength. However, the degree of aberration can vary significantly with wavelength in an optical system. 2. Astigmatism Due to Asymmetry: This form arises when the optical system lacks symmetry about the optical axis. This may be intentional, as in the case of cylindrical lenses, or due to manufacturing defects or misalignment of components. In such cases, astigmatism can be observed even for rays originating from on-axis object points. This type of astigmatism is particularly significant in ophthalmology, as imperfections in the cornea or lens of the human eye often lead to this aberration. Third-Order Astigmatism In analyzing third-order astigmatism, rays from a given point on the object are considered in two specific planes: Tangential Plane: This plane includes both the object point and the axis of symmetry. Rays propagating in this plane are called tangential rays. Planes containing the optical axis are referred to as meridional planes. For simplicity, object points are often chosen in the vertical (y) plane, which is sometimes called the meridional plane. Sagittal Plane: This plane is orthogonal to the tangential plane and contains the object point while intersecting the optical axis at the entrance pupil of the optical system. It contains the chief ray but not the optical axis, making it a skew plane rather than a meridional plane. Rays propagating in this plane are called sagittal rays. In third-order astigmatism, the sagittal and tangential rays form foci at different distances along the optical axis, known as the sagittal focus and tangential focus, respectively. An off-axis object point is not sharply imaged by the optical system. Instead, sharp lines are formed at these two foci. Between these foci, a round but blurry image is formed, referred to as the medial focus or the circle of least confusion. This plane often represents the best compromise for image location in systems with astigmatism. The degree of aberration due to astigmatism is proportional to the square of the angle between the rays from the object and the optical axis. With careful design, optical systems can be engineered to minimize or eliminate astigmatism, and such systems are called anastigmats. Astigmatism in Non-Rotationally Symmetric Systems If an optical system lacks axisymmetry, either due to errors in the shape of the optical surfaces or misalignment of components, astigmatism can occur even for on-axis object points. This effect is sometimes deliberately used in complex optical systems, such as certain types of telescopes. In analyzing these systems, tangential rays and rays in a meridional plane perpendicular to the tangential plane (called the sagittal meridional plane) are often considered. Ophthalmic Astigmatism In ophthalmology, the vertical and horizontal planes are identified as tangential and sagittal meridians, respectively. Ophthalmic astigmatism is a refractive error of the eye where there is a difference in the degree of refraction between different meridians. It is typically caused by an aspherical, non-revolutionary cornea, where the corneal profile slope and refractive power in one meridian are greater than those in the perpendicular axis. Astigmatism can make it difficult to see fine details. In some cases, vertical lines and objects, such as walls, may appear tilted to the patient, resembling the leaning Tower of Pisa. Astigmatism is often corrected using glasses with cylindrical lenses, contact lenses, or refractive surgery. It is a common condition, affecting approximately one in three people, and its prevalence increases with age. While mild astigmatism may go unnoticed, higher degrees can cause blurry vision, squinting, eye strain (asthenopia), fatigue, or headaches. Various tests are used by ophthalmologists and optometrists to detect and quantify astigmatism, including Snellen charts, keratometers, corneal topographers, autorefractors, retinoscopy, and Jackson cross cylinders in a phoropter. A clock dial or sunburst chart may also be used to determine the astigmatic axis and power. Astigmatism Due to Misaligned or Malformed Lenses and Mirrors The grinding and polishing of precision optical parts often involve significant downward pressure, which creates frictional side pressures during polishing strokes. These forces can flex and distort the parts, leading to astigmatic distortions that may become permanently polished into the surface if the underlying issues are not corrected. Such distortions lack rotational symmetry and can degrade optical system performance. The degree of distortion increases with the aspect ratio of the part (diameter to thickness ratio). Thicker lenses with lower aspect ratios (e.g., 4:1 to 6:1) flex less than high-aspect-ratio parts like optical windows, which can have aspect ratios of 15:1 or higher. The combination of surface or wavefront error precision requirements and part aspect ratio determines the degree of back support uniformity needed, especially during high-pressure polishing. Optical work often involves a degree of randomness that helps preserve rotationally symmetric surfaces, provided the part does not flex during the grinding or polishing process. Deliberate Astigmatism in Optical Systems Some optical systems intentionally incorporate astigmatism for specific purposes. For example, compact disc players use an astigmatic lens for focusing. When one axis is more in focus than the other, dot-like features on the disc appear as oval shapes. The orientation of the oval indicates which axis is more in focus and guides the lens movement to achieve optimal focus. A square arrangement of four sensors can detect this bias and adjust the lens position without being misled by oblong pits or other features on the disc surface. Similarly, some telescopes use deliberately astigmatic optics for specific applications.
